explanations.explanation: Yep. Verse 11 says Jehoshabeath, King Jehoram's daughter and the wife of Jehoiada the priest, was Ahaziah's sister. Ahaziah was Joash's father and the king of Judah. So the one who snatched little Joash away was his own father's sister. Family trees get tangled fast, baker.

Close, friend, but no. The verse says Jehoshabeath was the wife of Jehoiada the priest, not of Ahaziah. Ahaziah was Joash's father and a king of Judah. To him, she was his sister. Easy to cross those wires when so many names come flying at you.

Good thinking, baker, because she really is Joash's aunt. But this question asks about Joash's father, Ahaziah, and to him she was his sister (2 Chronicles 22:11). She is also the daughter of King Jehoram. So you spotted the right person, and the question just asks about her from Ahaziah's side. I've mixed up worse with a measuring cup.

That's it. Verse 12 says Joash remained hidden with them in the house of God. Jehoiada was a priest, so I think that put him right where Jehoiada worked. Earlier, Jehoshabeath had put him and his nurse in a bedroom (2 Chronicles 22:11). A tiny king tucked away in a bedroom, friend, and the whole thing stayed quiet.

Nope, baker. The text says Joash stayed hidden with them in the house of God, not in the palace. He is seated on the royal throne in the palace later (2 Chronicles 23:20). So the palace is where he ends up, not where he hides.

A mountain getaway sounds nice, friend, but that's not what the verse says. Joash remained hidden with them in the house of God (2 Chronicles 22:12). Earlier, he and his nurse were put in a bedroom (2 Chronicles 22:11). No hills mentioned. I've hidden in worse spots, and my last one was a junk drawer.

Six it is. Verse 12 says Joash remained hidden for six years while Athaliah ruled the land. Athaliah was Ahaziah's mother, the one who set out to destroy the royal heirs (2 Chronicles 22:10). Then in the seventh year, Jehoiada makes his move (2 Chronicles 23:1). Six years of waiting, baker, is a LONG time.

Three is a good round number, friend, but this wait was twice that. Verse 12 says Joash remained hidden for six years while Athaliah, Ahaziah's mother, ruled the land. Then comes the seventh year (2 Chronicles 23:1). Six years is a lot of patience in anybody's kitchen.

Twelve is a big swing, baker. The verse says six years, and then in the seventh year Jehoiada gets to work (2 Chronicles 23:1). During those six years, Athaliah, Ahaziah's mother, ruled the land (2 Chronicles 22:12). Half of twelve gets you there.

Right on. Verse 2 says they gathered the Levites from all the cities of Judah, along with the heads of the families of Israel. The Levites were the ones who served at the house of God, and Jehoiada was a priest, so they were his kind of crowd. Then they all came to Jerusalem. That's a lot of road trips for one plan, baker.

Gibeonites aren't named anywhere in this passage, friend. Verse 2 says the Levites were the ones gathered from all the cities of Judah. They came along with the heads of the families of Israel. Then the whole assembly made a covenant with the king in the house of God (2 Chronicles 23:3). Stick with the Levites on this one.

That's a fun name, baker, but this passage never mentions it. Verse 2 says they gathered the Levites from all the cities of Judah, plus the heads of Israel's families. Once everyone reached Jerusalem, the whole assembly made a covenant with the king in the house of God (2 Chronicles 23:3). The Levites are the answer here.

explanations.answer: The LORD promised it to David's line
explanations.explanation: Exactly. Jehoiada says, “He must reign, just as the LORD promised concerning the descendants of David.” (2 Chronicles 23:3) So the reason is a promise, and the promise came from the LORD. Joash was a descendant of David, and he was the king's son. The whole plan rests on that, baker.

explanations.answer: He was born in the house of God
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but the text never says Joash was born there. He was hidden in the house of God (2 Chronicles 22:12), which is a different thing. Jehoiada's reason is that the LORD promised the throne to David's descendants (2 Chronicles 23:3). Hiding somewhere doesn't make you king, or I'd be running a drawer kingdom.

explanations.answer: Athaliah once named him her heir
explanations.explanation: Not a chance, baker. The only thing this passage says Athaliah did about the royal heirs was set out to annihilate them (2 Chronicles 22:10). Jehoiada gives his reason instead: “He must reign, just as the LORD promised concerning the descendants of David.” (2 Chronicles 23:3) The promise did the work here, not her.

That's right. Jehoiada says, “No one is to enter the house of the LORD except the priests and those Levites who serve…” (2 Chronicles 23:6). He adds that they may enter because they are consecrated. Everyone else is to obey the requirement of the LORD. A short guest list, friend, and he means it.

This one is true, baker. Verse 6 says, “No one is to enter the house of the LORD except the priests and those Levites who serve…” The reason given is that they are consecrated. The rest of the people are to obey the requirement of the LORD. So the door really was only for the priests and serving Levites.

Not this time, friend. Verse 8 says Jehoiada had not released any of the divisions. So each of them took his men, those coming on duty on the Sabbath and those going off duty. Nobody clocked out early. I can't even get a timer to listen to me like that.

Correct. The text says, “…for Jehoiada the priest had not released any of the divisions.” (2 Chronicles 23:8) So each of them took his men, both those coming on duty and those going off. That's a full house, baker.

You got it, baker. Verse 9 says Jehoiada gave the commanders the spears and the large and small shields of King David that were in the house of God. David was the one the LORD made the promise about (2 Chronicles 23:3). Those weapons were still there waiting. Somebody kept them better than I kept my edges.

Saul is a fair guess, friend, but he's not the one in this verse. Verse 9 says these were the spears and shields of King David that were in the house of God. David is also the king whose descendants the LORD promised the throne to (2 Chronicles 23:3). Mixing up old kings is easy to do.

Solomon, David's son (2 Samuel 12:24), is a reasonable guess, baker. But verse 9 names King David as the owner of those spears and shields. They were kept in the house of God until Jehoiada handed them out. So the weapons come from the father, not the son.

That's the one. Verse 11 says Jehoiada and his sons brought out the king's son and put the crown on him. They also presented him with the Testimony, proclaimed him king and anointed him, and they shouted, “Long live the king!” Hidden for six years, then crowned, baker. Talk about a glow-up.

An ephod sounds official, friend, but this verse doesn't mention one. It says they put the crown on Joash. They also gave him the Testimony and anointed him (2 Chronicles 23:11). Jehoiada was the priest in this story, and the king got the crown.

Armor makes sense with all those weapons around, baker. But the text has them put the crown on him. The men with weapons in hand were surrounding the king (2 Chronicles 23:10). Joash himself got a crown, the Testimony and an anointing (2 Chronicles 23:11). The soldiers handled the weapons.

That's what she does. Verse 13 says Athaliah tore her clothes and screamed, “Treason, treason!” She walked in and saw the king by his pillar, the trumpeters and the rejoicing crowd. I think she did not get the welcome she was expecting. Quite the entrance, friend.

explanations.answer: Bows down before the new king
explanations.explanation: No bowing, baker. Verse 13 says she tore her clothes and screamed, “Treason, treason!” She had walked into a crowd that was rejoicing and blowing trumpets for the new king. Joash was standing by his pillar at the entrance, and she had ruled the land for six years (2 Chronicles 22:12). Bowing was not her move.

She doesn't sneak away, friend. Verse 13 says she tore her clothes and screamed, “Treason, treason!” Later the commanders seize her as she reaches the entrance of the Horse Gate on the palace grounds (2 Chronicles 23:15). Quiet was not her style that day.

Not so, baker. Verse 14 gives the priest's words: “She must not be put to death in the house of the LORD.” So Jehoiada tells the commanders to bring her out between the ranks. Then she is seized at the Horse Gate on the palace grounds (2 Chronicles 23:15). It is a heavy moment, and the house of the LORD was kept out of it.

Right. The text says, “She must not be put to death in the house of the LORD.” (2 Chronicles 23:14) So Jehoiada sends the commanders to bring her out between the ranks. She is seized as she reaches the entrance of the Horse Gate on the palace grounds (2 Chronicles 23:15). This is a heavy part, friend.

That's right, baker. Verse 16 says Jehoiada made a covenant between himself and the king and the people that they would be the LORD's people. That means the priest, the king and the people are all in it together. A new king and a new promise, friend.

This one is true, friend. Verse 16 says Jehoiada made a covenant between himself and the king and the people that they would be the LORD's people. That sentence has a lot of moving parts, so I get why it looks tricky. I second-guess my own recipe cards the same way.

You got it. Verse 17 says all the people went to the temple of Baal and tore it down. They smashed the altars and idols to pieces, too. Baal was a false god, and his temple, altars and idols all came down. That's a lot of smashing, baker.

A lock would be too gentle, friend. Verse 17 says the people tore the temple of Baal down and smashed the altars and idols to pieces. Locking things up is what I do with the cookie jar, not what happened here. This was a teardown.

Repurposing is a smart idea in my kitchen, baker, but not here. Verse 17 says the people tore the temple of Baal down. They also smashed the altars and idols to pieces. There was no building left to fill with boxes.

Right on. Verse 18 says Jehoiada put the oversight of the house of the LORD into the hands of the Levitical priests, whom David had appointed over the house of the LORD. Their job was to offer burnt offerings to the LORD as written in the Law of Moses. They were to do it with rejoicing and song, as ordained by David. The right people for the right job, baker.

The commanders do a lot in this story, baker, but that's not this job. Verse 18 says Jehoiada put the oversight of the house of the LORD into the hands of the Levitical priests. David had appointed them. The commanders were sent to bring Athaliah out (2 Chronicles 23:14), so they had their hands full already.

The nobles do show up, friend, but later. Verse 20 has them going with Jehoiada as they bring the king down to the palace. The oversight of the house of the LORD went to the Levitical priests, whom David had appointed (2 Chronicles 23:18). So it was handed to the ones David chose.

Not quite, friend. Verse 19 says Jehoiada stationed gatekeepers at the gates of the house of the LORD, so that no one who was in any way unclean could enter. That is not an open-door policy. The gates had people watching them.

That's right. Verse 19 says Jehoiada stationed gatekeepers at the gates of the house of the LORD, so that no one who was in any way unclean could enter. The gates were watched, not wide open. Even my bakery has a door policy, baker.

You got it. Verse 20 says they seated King Joash on the royal throne. They had brought him down from the house of the LORD and into the palace through the Upper Gate. He was a boy hidden in a bedroom six years before (2 Chronicles 22:12). Now look at him, baker.

A chariot would be a fun ride, friend, but the verse doesn't have one. It says they seated King Joash on the royal throne. That happened inside the palace after they entered through the Upper Gate (2 Chronicles 23:20). A king sits on a throne, baker.

A platform is close, baker, but the text has something fancier. Verse 20 says they seated King Joash on the royal throne. Earlier he was standing by his pillar at the entrance (2 Chronicles 23:13). Now he's seated where a king is supposed to sit.

Yes. Verse 21 says all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet, because Athaliah had been put to the sword. Earlier in the passage it was loud with trumpets and cheering (2 Chronicles 23:13). Now things settle down. Quiet after all that noise, friend, I know that feeling after a big batch.

Not restless, baker. Verse 21 says the people rejoiced and the city was quiet. The text gives the reason: Athaliah had been put to the sword. So after all the shouting and trumpets (2 Chronicles 23:13), things went calm.

The text doesn't say afraid, friend. Verse 21 says all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet. It adds that Athaliah had been put to the sword. So the word the text gives is quiet, not afraid.
